newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia said on world power shopping lists.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia said on world power shopping lists.

text.p: International power industry players are looking at mergers, acquisitions and other entry deals in the Australian states of Queensland, New South Wales and South Australia, a utilities expert said on Wednesday.

Chris Nichols, director utilities of accounting firm Price Waterhouse, told the Electricity Supply Association of Australia annual conference this reflected a globalising energy market in which big players were prepared to do "astonishingly big deals".
"Some (players) around the world are taking on characteristics of predators while others are taking on charactersitics of prey," Nichols said.
Accelerated entry to Australia by world power giants would follow big moves into the state of Victoria in 1996 as part of that state's A$13.0 billion privatisation of electricity assets.
Entrants to Victoria this year have included Edison Mission Energy, a unit of U.S.-based Edison International, and Britain's National Power Plc and Powergen Plc.

Earlier at the conference, Michael Sargent, chief executive of Canberra-based ACTEW Corp Ltd, said that the small size of the Australian market could make Australian utilities in a de-regulated market takeover victims.
Nichols said US$70.0 billion in merger and acquisition activity had occurred in the world power industry in the past 15-20 months - "pretty exciting stuff".
"Executives believe that if you don't do something to someone, they will do something to you," he said. The trend was global, not confined to the U.S. and Britain, he said.
It incorporated not just acquisitions and mergers but diversification, with energy players moving into telecommunications, real estate and other areas, he said.
The biggest diversification, however, was into energy-related areas, he said.
Australian disaggregation was creating very small power industry businesses in the cause of competition, he said.
Nichols said he felt the market could drive consolidation among these businesses and asked whether businesses would want to maintain smallness to maintain competition benchmarks.
